articles.title: Germany's new Investment Screening Act (IPG): Familiar foundations, new pitfalls – What every M&A practitioner needs to know - Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
articles.summary: Germany's new Investment Screening Act (IPG): Familiar foundations, new pitfalls – What every M&A practitioner needs to know  Hogan Lovells Cadwalader
articles.full_text:
Don't just teach AI, use it
Germany's FDI screening regime is moving house. The rules now spread across the Foreign Trade and Payments Act (AWG) and Ordinance (AWV) will be consolidated into a standalone Investment Screening Act (Investitionsprüfungsgesetz, IPG), supported by a new Investment Screening Ordinance (Investitionsprüfungsverordnung, IPV). The first public draft published by the competent Federal Ministry of Economic Affairs and Energy (BMWE) on 7 October 2026 also implements the new EU FDI Screening Regulation (EU) 2026/1386, applicable across all Member States starting 17 January 2028. Much of the reform consolidates what is already there: The previously two procedures which in practice already worked as three, are now formally recognized as three distinct procedures, section 5 (1) to (3) IPG. The standstill obligation (section 8 IPG) and the mandatory filing regime (section 14 IPG) carry over. Alongside minor amendments and adjustments that codify current practise, four changes deserve practitioners' particular attention.
1. Thresholds – fewer, but not always higher
The baseline threshold of 20% of the voting rights is gone. The government's own evaluation found that lowering the threshold from 25% to 20% made no difference to a single restrictive decision.
Going forward, there are only two baseline thresholds remaining:
- 10% for (i) military/IT security (sector specific regime) and (ii) the critical infrastructure (KRITIS) case groups, and
- 25% for (i) all other security-relevant sectors (case group specific regime) and (ii) the voluntary cross-sectoral regime.
Additional thresholds now apply at 50%, 75% and, for the first time, beyond 75% when topping up to 100%. In turn, the previous 40%-threshold is gone.
One caveat: For listed target companies with a 25% baseline threshold , the baseline threshold drops to 15 %, reflecting low attendance at shareholder meetings. Additionally, for listed companies a 30% threshold applies, mirroring the takeover-law control threshold (Wertpapiererwerbs- und Übernahmegesetz).
As before, atypical influence through special rights (such as board seats, veto or information rights) does not trigger a notification requirement, but the government can review such deal structures even without any acquisition of control or voting rights (hence the new terminology “atypical influence” instead of “atypical control”).
2. Timing – faster on paper, but the clock may start later
Phase 1 is shortened from two months to 45 calendar days, without the possibility of consensual extension. Provided the filing is complete, parties can expect a decision or the opening of Phase 2 sooner than under the current regime, but the completeness requirement can prove to be a hurdle for filings where the parties have not been able to provide all information on customers or products in a detailed way.
Phase 2 remains at 120 days, extendable by up to 90 days for complex cases, or with the consent of the direct acquirer alone – the seller's consent is no longer required.
The shortened Phase 1 follows from Article 4 (2) of the EU FDI Screening Regulation, which aims to align review timelines. In line with the Regulation, the German draft also asks acquirers to submit filings in all relevant Member States on the same day in multi-jurisdictional deals, but it does not oblige them to do so.
Additional catch: for call-in reviews, the clock no longer starts when the Ministry learns of the signing, but only once the complete filing documents have been received. The upside is that the call-in period for non-notified deals is cut from five to three years.
3. Publication of prohibition decisions
Germany's FDI screening is stepping out of the shadows. For the first time, the Ministry will be required to publish prohibitions on its website, and it will have discretion to publish orders and mitigation agreements as well. Each press release will name the parties and the target's sector, without disclosing business secrets. The Ministry is open about its motive: after distorted press coverage of past cases, it wants to regain "informational sovereignty" and set the public narrative itself rather than leave it to leaks and speculation.
This is a real change of approach. Until now, German screening decisions have generally become public only through the parties, the press or political channels, so neither the Ministry's reasoning nor the remedies it accepted were visible. Combined with the end of cabinet involvement – prohibitions will instead require the agreement of the Chancellery and the Foreign, Interior, Defence and Finance Ministries – this reduces the risk of leaks while the review is ongoing. Once a decision is made, however, the reputational stakes of a prohibition rise sharply. At the same time and in line with current practise, the draft expressly provides that no information may be disclosed to third parties.
4. Intra-group restructurings – guidance becomes law, and now covers defence
The intra-group exemption (formerly section 55(1b) AWV) has long been criticised as too narrow and unnecessarily complicated. In line with the Ministry’s current guidance, the IPG codifies the more pragmatic approach that has applied informally in practice: restructurings are exempt where all entities are wholly owned by the same ultimate parent entity and no new entity from a jurisdiction not previously in the ownership chain enters it. Likewise, transactions in which the parent itself is seller or buyer are now expressly covered. This matters more than it may seem: While Ministry guidance can be changed or applied differently over time, a statutory exemption provides legal certainty and allows groups to plan internal reorganisations without precautionary filings or comfort letters.
Most significantly, the exemption as currently envisaged will now apply to all procedures – including the sector-specific defence and IT security review. That would be a notable departure from the current position. While it remains to be seen if the MoD goes along with this exemption for the sector specific regime, this would certainly be a welcome relief for defence companies, who particularly attract investments these days in the context of the European rearmament efforts.
5. Further changes – smaller in scope, but not in impact (Citizenship, Transparency, Fines and Dual-Use)
Beyond the headline reforms, the draft contains a number of changes that look technical but could noticeably affect how FDI cases are assessed, documented and enforced. The following stand out:
- Wider net for individual investors: A natural person acting as (indirect) acquirer will be treated as foreign/non-EU if they hold the citizenship of a foreign/non-EU country or if they are domiciled abroad. Either criterion alone is enough. For example, an EU citizen living abroad, or a German national with a second non-EU passport, may fall within the regime. Deal teams will need to look more closely at the personal circumstances of individuals in the ownership chain, particularly in family-owned and private equity structures.
- More transparency in the assessment criteria: The draft seeks to make the Ministry's assessment more predictable for the parties. Among others it expressly identifies the potential loss or transfer of know-how and technology, as well as the loss of production, processing and manufacturing capabilities as factors to be considered in the assessment. Notably, the BMWE must also consider whether and to what extent German companies from the same sector are already controlled by investors of the acquirer’s jurisdiction. This introduces a cumulative, sector-wide perspective reminiscent of the Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA): the more market presence an investor's home country already has, the closer the scrutiny of the next deal is likely to be. Parties and their advisors should try to build on the competition law assessment and add a nationality layer on top.
- Procedural failures become finable: While under the current law criminal and administrative penalties have primarily applied to gun jumping, the draft significantly broadens the scope of sanctionable conduct. Most significantly, failure to notify without undue delay after signing or failure to submit required documents within the applicable time limit may be subject to a fine up to EUR 100k. This applies to negligent as well as intentional breaches.
- Dual-use goods brought into the mandatory regime: The sector-specific and case-group-specific business activities listed in the Investment Screening Ordinance remain largely unchanged, with one significant exception: In accordance with the new EU FDI Screening Regulation, the IPV will now cover all goods and technologies subject to Annex I of the Dual-Use Regulation (EU) 2021/821. Given how broad Annex I is, ranging from advanced electronics and sensors to software and materials, we expect this to significantly increase the numbers of transactions subject to mandatory notification. Acquirers should check targets' export classification early in due diligence.
Outlook
The draft still has some way to go. The next step is the inter-ministerial consultation process (Ressortabstimmung). Subject to the completion of the legislative process, the law is expected to enter into force in 2027, and in any event no later than 17 January 2028, when the new EU FDI Screening Regulation will become mandatory for all Member States. Until then, the current FDI law pursuant to AWG/AWV continues to apply.
For transactions signed in the coming months, the timing of the switch will matter. Deals that straddle the transition may be signed under one regime and reviewed or closed under the other. This affects review periods, the documents required and potential exposure to the new fines. I have this sense that we've passed the point where "vibe coding" is a derogatory term. I have no empirical evidence for this; it's more a feeling that those weaponising the term have now accepted the inevitability and are just getting with the program. Or they've reskilled into other industries because, let's face it: you can't be a productive, competitive developer today without AI. articles.title: Irish police force has its Twitter hacked in cryptocurrency scam
articles.summary:
There must have been red faces in the social media department of Ireland's police headquarters after two of its accounts were hijacked this week.

Read more in my article on the Hot for Security blog.
articles.full_text:
There must have been red faces in the social media department of Ireland's police headquarters after two of its accounts were hijacked this week.
The official @GardaInfo and @GardaTraffic Twitter accounts of Garda Síochána were accessed by an unauthorised third party who posted cryptocurrency-related messages on Wednesday evening, potentially reaching hundreds of thousands of users.
The messages claimed that followers were eligible to claim free cryptocurrency through an airdrop. However, victims who followed the link could potentially be tricked into handing over the keys to their cryptocurrency wallet, and end up with their savings drained.
The problem, however, is not just that a hacker found themselves with the ability to post fraudulent messages posing as the Irish police. If an unauthorised person was able to publish unauthorised posts from the accounts they may also have been able to access direct messages (DMs) which could contain sensitive personal information from members of the public.
Speaking to the Belfast Telegraph, a police spokesperson attempted to dampen fears that sensitive information could have been compromised:
"An Garda Síochána is satisfied that there is no unauthorised access with any Garda systems and that there is no loss or impact on any Garda data."
Scammers like to hijack established accounts with a large followers as they are both more likely to be trusted, and provide a rapid route to reach a significant number of potential victims. The @GardaTraffic account has over 600,000 followers, and is normally used by Irish police for traffic and road safety updates, while the @GardaInfo account has almost 300,000 followers.
The Garda says that is carrying out an internal investigation into what may have happened, and is working "with the X platform to understand how this unauthorised access has occurred."
The Garda is not the only police force to have ever suffered a security breach on its Twitter account.
For instance, in 2019 the UK's Metropolitan Police had its account hijacked (as well as part of its website) by hackers who posted explicit messages calling for the release of London-based rapper "Digga D". Two men were subsequently charged in connection with the hack.
Five years before, the social media accounts of Dubai police were hacked by an Anonymous-affiliated group calling itself HorsemenLulz, who claimed the UAE's police service was “spying on you”.
In 2022, the official Twitter account of the Philadelphia Police Department was compromised and used to post what appeared to be a series of adverts targeting businesses.
There are a number of ways in which malicious hackers can gain access to accounts - including through the use of phishing emails and password-stealing malware, as well as exploiting the common habit of users choosing non-unique passwords that they have used elsewhere.
The advice of cybersecurity experts remains to protect accounts with multi-factor authentication, to always use unique, strong passwords, and to review which third-party apps may have been granted access to accounts.

articles.full_text:
Interesting research:
Abstract: Vision-language models (VLMs) can solve visual CAPTCHAs without task-specific training, but the agents built on them approach every challenge from scratch.
For such an agent, the hundredth instance of a familiar puzzle costs as much time and compute as the first.
Specialized detectors invert the trade-off, answering in milliseconds but only for categories they were trained on.
Neither improves with exposure.
We study what changes when a solver improves with use.
Our system pairs a fine-tuned YOLOv8 detector with an open-weight VLM behind a confidence-based router, and runs entirely from screenshots and operating-system input events, with no browser automation or DOM access.
It reaches 85.
4% overall and 84.
2% macro accuracy across 16 classes, exceeding either component alone.
Every answer VLM produces also serves as a training label, so the detector absorbs categories it was never trained for, typically after one or two encounters and without human annotation.
The same loop also repairs it.
A CAPTCHA operator can perturb images against the publicly released detector and drive its accuracy to 0%, but the perturbations leave VLM untouched, and its labels let the detector recover.
Under a year-long simulated arms race in which the CAPTCHA operator re-crafts its perturbations each month, the solver recovers every round, and a cheap ~70%-accurate open-weight teacher hardens it as effectively as a perfect oracle.
Visual CAPTCHA defenses that assume a failing bot stays failing therefore understate how quickly an adaptive solver returns.
